claim: Neuropathic pain affects approximately 10% of the population.
source: It affects ~10% of the population (van Hecke et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to van Hecke et al., 2014

claim: Neuropathic pain is difficult to treat.
source: and is notoriously difficult to treat (Woolf, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolf, 2010

claim: Mechanical allodynia can be acutely reproduced by blocking synaptic inhibition at the spinal level.
source: This so-called mechanical allodynia can be acutely reproduced by blocking synaptic inhibition at the spinal level (Miraucourt et al., 2009; Sivilotti and Woolf, 1994; Sorkin and Puig, 1996; Sorkin et al., 1998; Yaksh, 1989).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Synaptic inhibition in the spinal dorsal horn is reduced after nerve injury.
source: Numerous other studies have shown that synaptic inhibition in the spinal dorsal horn is reduced after nerve injury (for reviews, see Prescott, 2015; Price et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: Disinhibition can result from reduced current flow through activated receptors due to dysregulation of intracellular chloride caused by KCC2 hypofunction.
source: but the latter stems uniquely from dysregulation of intracellular chloride due to KCC2 hypofunction (Coull et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coull et al., 2003

claim: Enhancing KCC2 function reverses injury-induced allodynia.
source: Enhancing KCC2 function reverses injury-induced allodynia (Gagnon et al., 2013; Lavertu et al., 2014; Mapplebeck et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Chloride dysregulation contributes significantly to injury-induced disinhibition.
source: thus demonstrating that chloride dysregulation contributes significantly to injury-induced disinhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the reversal of allodynia by enhancing KCC2 function

claim: Chloride dysregulation has been shown to occur in dorsal horn neurons with different spiking patterns.
source: Chloride dysregulation has been shown to occur in dorsal horn neurons with different spiking patterns (Coull et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Coull et al., 2003

claim: Disinhibition unmasks low-threshold input to projection neurons that normally respond exclusively to noxious input.
source: Disinhibition is known to unmask low-threshold input to projection neurons that normally respond exclusively to noxious input (Baba et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2017; Keller et al., 2007; Lavertu et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2013; Miraucourt et al., 2007; Miraucourt et al., 2009; Torsney and MacDermott, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Low-threshold input is conveyed polysynaptically to projection neurons via excitatory interneurons.
source: Low-threshold input is conveyed polysynaptically to projection neurons via excitatory interneurons (for reviews, see Duan et al., 2018; Peirs and Seal, 2016; Prescott et al., 2014; Takazawa and MacDermott, 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: Excitatory interneurons are necessary for mechanical allodynia.
source: Separate work indicates that excitatory interneurons are necessary for mechanical allodynia (Cheng et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2006; Malmberg et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Inhibitory neurons receive inhibitory input.
source: Inhibitory neurons also receive inhibitory input (Takazawa and MacDermott, 2010a; Zheng et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Many neurons have a receptive field with an excitatory center and inhibitory surround.
source: As originally described in retinal cells by Kuffler (1953), many neurons have an RF with an excitatory center and inhibitory surround. This includes dorsal horn neurons (Hillman and Wall, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuffler (1953) and Hillman and Wall (1969)

claim: Reduced two-point discrimination in patients with neuropathic pain is consistent with increased RF overlap.
source: Notwithstanding other explanations, reduced two-point discrimination in patients with neuropathic pain (Pleger et al., 2006) is consistent with increased RF overlap that could occur if surround inhibition is lost and RFs expand.
evidence: Inference based on citation to Pleger et al., 2006

claim: Receptive fields expand after nerve injury.
source: Animal studies have demonstrated that RFs expand after nerve injury (Behbehani and Dollberg-Stolik, 1994; Cumberbatch et al., 1998; Devor and Wall, 1981; Suzuki et al., 2000; Tabo et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: KCC2 blockade significantly increased firing evoked by stimulation in the RF center.
source: KCC2 blockade significantly increased firing evoked by stimulation in the RF center or surround (Z = 4.79, p<0.001 and Z = 4.72, p<0.001 respectively; Wilcoxon tests) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: KCC2 blockade significantly increased firing evoked by stimulation in the RF surround.
source: KCC2 blockade significantly increased firing evoked by stimulation in the RF center or surround (Z = 4.79, p<0.001 and Z = 4.72, p<0.001 respectively; Wilcoxon tests) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: After disinhibition caused by KCC2 blockade, neurons were driven more strongly by unmasked excitatory input from the RF surround than by enhanced input from the RF center.
source: Hence, after disinhibition caused by KCC2 blockade, neurons were driven more strongly by unmasked excitatory input from the RF surround than by enhanced input from the RF center.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data analysis in Figure 1E

claim: Some units had a monophasic spike waveform whereas others had a biphasic waveform.
source: Over the course of these experiments we noticed that some units had a monophasic spike waveform whereas others had a biphasic waveform (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from experimental recordings shown in Figure 2A

claim: Units with monophasic waveforms exhibited spike rate adaptation during sustained tactile stimulation whereas units with biphasic waveforms did not.
source: The former exhibited spike rate adaptation during sustained tactile stimulation with a von Frey (VF) filament whereas the latter did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observation from experimental recordings shown in Figure 2B

claim: The adaptation time constant differed significantly between units classified by their spike waveform.
source: The adaptation time constant measured from exponential-rise-to-maximum fits of the cumulative probability distribution of spike times from each unit differed significantly between units classified by their spike waveform (T23 = 8.58, p<0.001; unpaired t-test) (Figure 2B inset).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B inset

claim: Adapting units had a significantly smaller RF than non-adapting units at baseline.
source: The RFs of adapting units were significantly smaller than RFs of non-adapting units at baseline (U = 17.5, p=0.013; Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: KCC2 blockade enlarged RFs in both adapting units and non-adapting units.
source: KCC2 blockade enlarged RFs in both adapting units (Q14 = 11.69, p<0.001; SNK test) and non-adapting units (Q6 = 5.94, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Adapting units receive tactile input exclusively from rapid-adapting (RA) afferents.
source: According to this analysis, adapting units receive tactile input exclusively from RA afferents whereas non-adapting units receive tactile input preferentially from SA afferents (Figure 2E).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cross-correlogram analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Non-adapting units receive tactile input preferentially from slow-adapting (SA) afferents.
source: According to this analysis, adapting units receive tactile input exclusively from RA afferents whereas non-adapting units receive tactile input preferentially from SA afferents (Figure 2E).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cross-correlogram analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Projection neurons are absent in lamina II and represent only approximately 5% of neurons in lumbar segments of lamina I in rats.
source: Since projection neurons are absent in lamina II and represent only ~5% of neurons in lumbar segments of lamina I in rats (Spike et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Spike et al., 2003

claim: Approximately 2/3 of local interneurons in the superficial dorsal horn are excitatory and 1/3 are inhibitory.
source: of which approximately 2/3 are excitatory and 1/3 are inhibitory (Abraira et al., 2017; Polgár et al., 2003; Prescott and Ratté, 2012; Todd, 2010; Todd, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Metabotropic glutamate receptor five is expressed almost exclusively on excitatory neurons.
source: Metabotropic glutamate receptor five is expressed almost exclusively on excitatory neurons and its agonist 3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine (DHPG) has been shown to selectively modulate the excitability of excitatory neurons (Hu and Gereau, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu and Gereau, 2011

claim: DHPG preferentially affected adapting cells.
source: Comparing brush-evoked firing before and after intrathecal DHPG revealed that adapting cells were preferentially affected (χ2 = 9.95, p=0.007) (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Adapting cells are excitatory neurons.
source: consistent with adapting cells being excitatory neurons.
evidence: Inference based on DHPG preferentially affecting adapting cells and DHPG's known selectivity for excitatory neurons

claim: The somatostatin receptor sst2a is expressed selectively on inhibitory neurons.
source: The somatostatin (SST) receptor sst2a is expressed selectively on inhibitory neurons (Todd et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Todd et al., 1998

claim: Intrathecal application of SST preferentially affected brush-evoked spiking in non-adapting cells.
source: Intrathecal application of SST preferentially affected brush-evoked spiking in non-adapting cells (χ2 = 16.85, p<0.001) (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Non-adapting cells are inhibitory neurons.
source: consistent with non-adapting cells being inhibitory neurons.
evidence: Inference based on SST preferentially affecting non-adapting cells and SST's known selectivity for inhibitory neurons

claim: The distributions of adapting and non-adapting units by depth were significantly different.
source: The distributions of adapting and non-adapting units were significantly different (D = 0.56, p<0.001; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The average depth of adapting units was 156 ± 72 μm.
source: with an average depth (± sd) of 156 ± 72 μm and 234 ± 57 μm, respectively (Figure 3C left)
evidence: Measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The average depth of non-adapting units was 234 ± 57 μm.
source: with an average depth (± sd) of 156 ± 72 μm and 234 ± 57 μm, respectively (Figure 3C left)
evidence: Measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: KCC2 blockade significantly increased i-o curve slope in adapting and non-adapting units.
source: KCC2 blockade significantly increased i-o curve slope in adapting and non-adapting units (Z = 3.82, p<0.001 and Z = 3.30, p<0.001, respectively; Wilcoxon tests) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Spontaneous firing was significantly greater in non-adapting units than in adapting units at baseline.
source: but separate analysis showed that spontaneous firing was significantly greater in non-adapting units than in adapting units at baseline (U = 116.5, p<0.001; Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: KCC2 blockade significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units.
source: and that KCC2 blockade significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units (Z = 3.58, p<0.001; Wilcoxon test) but not in adapting units (Z = 0.39, p=0.70) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: KCC2 blockade did not significantly increase spontaneous firing in adapting units.
source: and that KCC2 blockade significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units (Z = 3.58, p<0.001; Wilcoxon test) but not in adapting units (Z = 0.39, p=0.70) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons display no difference in chloride extrusion capacity.
source: Results revealed no difference in chloride extrusion capacity between excitatory and inhibitory neurons (T12 = 0.030, p=0.98, unpaired t-test) (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The A-type potassium current is selectively expressed in the spinal dorsal horn by excitatory neurons.
source: The A-type potassium current, which is associated with delayed- and single-spiking (Balachandar and Prescott, 2018), is selectively expressed in the spinal dorsal horn by excitatory neurons (Hu et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Tonic-spiking is observed almost exclusively in inhibitory neurons.
source: whereas tonic-spiking is observed almost exclusively in inhibitory neurons (Yasaka et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasaka et al., 2010

claim: Disinhibition significantly increased the slope in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Disinhibition significantly increased the slope in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Q5 = 6.62, p<0.001 and Q8 = 3.75, p=0.020, respectively; SNK tests) (Figure 6D top)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Disinhibition increased the y-intercept only in inhibitory neurons.
source: but increased the y-intercept only in inhibitory neurons (Q8 = 8.09, p<0.001 vs Q5 = 0.35, p=0.81 in excitatory neurons) (Figure 6D bottom).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Intrathecal BDNF significantly increased firing evoked by brush stimulation applied to the RF center of adapting and non-adapting units.
source: Intrathecal BDNF significantly increased firing evoked by brush stimulation applied to the RF center of adapting and non-adapting units (Z = 3.10, p<0.001 for both cell types; Wilcoxon tests) (Figure 7A left).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: BDNF-mediated enhancement of evoked firing was significantly reversed by subsequent application of ACTZ.
source: In all cases, BDNF-mediated enhancement of evoked firing was significantly reversed by subsequent application of ACTZ (Z ≥ 2.85, p≤0.002).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: BDNF failed to induce spontaneous firing in adapting units.
source: Moreover, BDNF failed to induce spontaneous firing in adapting units (Z = 0.51 p=0.64) but significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units (Z = 2.52, p=0.008) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: BDNF significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units.
source: Moreover, BDNF failed to induce spontaneous firing in adapting units (Z = 0.51 p=0.64) but significantly increased spontaneous firing in non-adapting units (Z = 2.52, p=0.008) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: BDNF causes comparable disinhibition in both adapting and non-adapting cell types.
source: These results demonstrate that BDNF causes comparable disinhibition in both cell types
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 7

claim: Stimulation in the RF surround significantly reduced the response to stimulation in the RF center under baseline conditions.
source: As predicted, stimulation in the RF surround significantly reduced the response to stimulation in the RF center (T22 = −9.26, p<0.001 and T11 = −2.90, p=0.014 for adapting and non-adapting units, respectively; one sample t-tests on log-transformed data) (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Adapting units experienced a significantly larger reduction from RF surround stimulation than non-adapting units under baseline conditions.
source: Adapting units experienced a significantly larger reduction than non-adapting units (Q33 = 3.61, p=0.013; SNK test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: After KCC2 blockade, the effect of stimulation in the RF surround was inverted and enhanced the response to stimulation in the RF center.
source: After KCC2 blockade, the effect of stimulation in the RF surround was inverted and enhanced the response to stimulation in the RF center (T22 = 6.24, p<0.001 and T11 = 6.06, p<0.001 for adapting and non-adapting units, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Adapting units experienced a significantly larger enhancement from RF surround stimulation than non-adapting units after KCC2 blockade.
source: Moreover, adapting units experienced a significantly larger enhancement than non-adapting units (Q33 = 2.91, p=0.044; SNK test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Adapting units receive strong excitatory input balanced by strong inhibitory input.
source: These data suggest that adapting units receive strong excitatory input balanced by strong inhibitory input, whereas non-adapting units receive weaker excitatory input balanced by weaker inhibitory input.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data in Figure 8

claim: Non-adapting units receive weaker excitatory input balanced by weaker inhibitory input.
source: These data suggest that adapting units receive strong excitatory input balanced by strong inhibitory input, whereas non-adapting units receive weaker excitatory input balanced by weaker inhibitory input.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data in Figure 8

claim: Excitatory neurons are more disinhibited than inhibitory neurons by chloride dysregulation in the spinal dorsal horn.
source: Excitatory neurons are more disinhibited than inhibitory neurons by chloride dysregulation in the spinal dorsal horn
evidence: Main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings

claim: Excitatory neurons rely more heavily on inhibition to counterbalance strong excitation than inhibitory neurons.
source: This is not because chloride is differentially dysregulated in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, but, rather, because excitatory neurons rely more heavily on inhibition to counterbalance strong excitation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Receptive fields in both excitatory and inhibitory cell types have a center-surround organization.
source: Receptive fields in both cell types have a center-surround organization but disinhibition unmasks more excitatory input to excitatory neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Disinhibition unmasks more excitatory input to excitatory neurons than to inhibitory neurons.
source: Receptive fields in both cell types have a center-surround organization but disinhibition unmasks more excitatory input to excitatory neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Differences in intrinsic excitability affect how chloride dysregulation affects spiking.
source: Differences in intrinsic excitability also affect how chloride dysregulation affects spiking.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Inhibitory neurons are subject to strong tonic inhibition.
source: Second, inhibitory neurons are subject to strong tonic inhibition (Gradwell et al., 2017; Takazawa and MacDermott, 2010a).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: BDNF is sufficient to downregulate KCC2 and cause allodynia in both male and female rodents.
source: we recently showed that BNDF is sufficient to downregulate KCC2 and cause allodynia in both male and female rodents (Mapplebeck et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mapplebeck et al., 2019

claim: Dynamic allodynia provoked by light brushing of the skin is a far greater clinical problem than the allodynia provoked by punctate stimuli or pressure.
source: Dynamic allodynia provoked by light brushing of the skin is a far greater clinical problem than the allodynia provoked by punctate stimuli or pressure (Hansson, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hansson, 2003

claim: Activating TrkB-ChR2-positive neurons provokes allodynia.
source: Dhandapani et al. (2018) showed that activating TrkB-ChR2-positive neurons – which include D-hair (Aδ) and RA afferents – provokes allodynia
evidence: Supported by citation to Dhandapani et al., 2018

claim: Activating Vglut1-ChR2-positive neurons does not provoke allodynia.
source: whereas Chamessian et al. (2019) showed that activating Vglut1-ChR2-positive neurons – which include RA and SA afferents – does not.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chamessian et al., 2019

claim: Activation of RA but not SA afferents produces allodynia.
source: The discrepancy suggests that activation of RA but not SA afferents produces allodynia
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing results of Dhandapani et al. (2018) and Chamessian et al. (2019)

claim: KCC2 is equally important for chloride regulation in males and female rodents.
source: In separate experiments, we have determined that KCC2 is equally important for chloride regulation in males and female rodents, and that KCC2 downregulation contributes equally to neuropathic pain in both sexes (Mapplebeck et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mapplebeck et al., 2019

claim: KCC2 downregulation contributes equally to neuropathic pain in both male and female rodents.
source: In separate experiments, we have determined that KCC2 is equally important for chloride regulation in males and female rodents, and that KCC2 downregulation contributes equally to neuropathic pain in both sexes (Mapplebeck et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mapplebeck et al., 2019

claim: Neurons operating as coincidence detectors respond preferentially to synchronous inputs.
source: Neurons operating as coincidence detectors respond preferentially to synchronous inputs (Ratté et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ratté et al., 2013

claim: RA afferents' spikes occur synchronously.
source: that are likely to arise from RA afferents whose spikes occur synchronously (Lankarany et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lankarany et al., 2019

claim: Neurons operating as integrators respond to asynchronous inputs.
source: whereas neurons operating as integrators also respond to asynchronous inputs that are likely to arise from SA afferents whose spikes occur asynchronously.
evidence: Inference based on established knowledge of neuronal integration

claim: Preprodynorphin neurons exhibit spontaneous spiking.
source: Spontaneous spiking has been previously reported in preprodynorphin neurons (Zhang et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: Preprodynorphin neurons express the sst2a receptor.
source: which express the sst2a receptor (Kardon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kardon et al., 2014

claim: sst2a receptor activation causes hyperpolarization via activation of an inward rectifying potassium current according to in vitro recordings.
source: Notably, sst2a receptor activation causes hyperpolarization via activation of an inward rectifying potassium current according to in vitro recordings (Kim et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2002

claim: Application of a high concentration of SST may cause receptor internalization and paradoxically reduce normal sst2a signaling.
source: but one possibility is that application of a high concentration of SST caused receptor internalization (Stroh et al., 2000) and paradoxically reduced normal sst2a signaling
evidence: Speculation based on citation to Stroh et al., 2000

claim: Excitatory neurons genetically identified by somatostatin expression exhibit delayed-, single-, or burst-spiking.
source: This is consistent with excitatory neurons genetically identified by somatostatin expression (most of which exhibit delayed-, single-, or burst-spiking) and inhibitory neurons genetically identified by dynorphin expression (most of which exhibit tonic- or burst-spiking) (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duan et al., 2014

claim: Inhibitory neurons genetically identified by dynorphin expression exhibit tonic- or burst-spiking.
source: This is consistent with excitatory neurons genetically identified by somatostatin expression (most of which exhibit delayed-, single-, or burst-spiking) and inhibitory neurons genetically identified by dynorphin expression (most of which exhibit tonic- or burst-spiking) (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duan et al., 2014

claim: Subthreshold depolarization is actively amplified and drives repetitive spiking in tonic-spiking inhibitory neurons.
source: First, because of voltage-gated currents, subthreshold depolarization is actively amplified and drives repetitive spiking in tonic-spiking inhibitory neurons but is actively attenuated and fails to drive repetitive spiking in single- and delayed-spiking excitatory neurons (Prescott and De Koninck, 2005; Ratté et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Subthreshold depolarization is actively attenuated and fails to drive repetitive spiking in single- and delayed-spiking excitatory neurons.
source: First, because of voltage-gated currents, subthreshold depolarization is actively amplified and drives repetitive spiking in tonic-spiking inhibitory neurons but is actively attenuated and fails to drive repetitive spiking in single- and delayed-spiking excitatory neurons (Prescott and De Koninck, 2005; Ratté et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Broader stimuli evoke greater inhibition in the visual system.
source: but it is entirely consistent with experiments in the visual system showing that broader stimuli evoke greater inhibition (Haider et al., 2010; Vinje and Gallant, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Dynamic allodynia required a set of neurons defined by the co-expression of VGLUT3 and Lbx1.
source: Cheng et al. (2017) recently found that dynamic allodynia required a set of neurons defined by the co-expression of VGLUT3 and Lbx1
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2017

claim: Hypersensitivity to von Frey stimulation persisted after ablation of VGLUT3/Lbx1 neurons.
source: whereas hypersensitivity to von Frey stimulation persisted after those neurons were ablated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2017

claim: Disinhibition caused by chloride dysregulation affects responses to both brush and von Frey stimuli.
source: Having tested with both brush and von Frey stimuli, our results show that disinhibition caused by chloride dysregulation affects responses to both types of stimuli

claim: Most (if not all) dorsal horn neurons are under inhibitory control.
